balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For NVR, Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For NVR, Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For NVR, Inc.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For NVR, Inc.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For NVR, Inc.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For NVR, Inc.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For NVR, Inc.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For NVR, Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

ordersBacklog.title: Net sales orders, closings and backlog
ordersBacklog.content:
Net sales orders are new contracts signed in the period, net of cancellations; homes closed are settlements that convert to revenue; backlog is the stock of signed-but-unclosed homes, the forward order book.

For NVR: backlog (homes) leads revenue by roughly two to three quarters because almost all homes are build-to-order, so this chart is the earliest read on where closings and revenue head next. Backlog fell every quarter through 2026 alongside weaker orders, which is why revenue guidance has turned cautious without a formal number.

What to watch:

  • Net orders accelerating or decelerating versus the prior-year quarter
  • Backlog shrinking even as closings hold up (a sign closings are about to slow)
  • The gap between orders and closings in a single quarter -- it is cancellations and timing, not demand destruction, if backlog barely moves

asp.title: Average selling price
asp.content:
Average selling price per home at new order, at settlement (closing) and in the backlog -- all in dollars per home, not millions.

For NVR: because the backlog and new-order ASPs lead the settlement ASP by a quarter or more (build-to-order), a new-order ASP falling below the backlog ASP is an early signal that incentives/discounting are rising or the mix is shifting to lower-priced product -- exactly the pricing pressure management has flagged through 2026.

What to watch:

  • New order ASP diverging below backlog/settlement ASP
  • All three ASPs falling together, which points to broad pricing pressure rather than mix

communitiesCancel.title: Active communities and cancellation rate
communitiesCancel.content:
Active communities is the count of open selling locations -- NVR's capacity to generate new orders. Cancellation rate is the share of signed contracts that buyers walk away from before closing.

For NVR: because NVR options rather than owns land, it can open or idle communities faster than a land-banking peer, so a flat or shrinking community count despite available lots is a demand call, not a land constraint. Rising cancellations alongside falling ASPs point to an affordability-driven buyer pullback rather than a one-off.

What to watch:

  • Community count growth stalling while lots controlled keeps rising (capacity being banked, not opened)
  • Cancellation rate above its historical high-teens norm

homeMarginLots.title: Home sales gross margin and lots controlled
homeMarginLots.content:
Home sales gross margin is homebuilding revenue less cost of homes sold (land, construction, variances), NVR's own segment-level profitability measure -- distinct from the consolidated gross/operating margin charted above because it strips out mortgage banking. Lots controlled is the pipeline of lots under option (owned plus optioned), the land-light model's capacity measure.

For NVR: this margin compressed every quarter of 2026 (23.7% FY2024 → 21.2% FY2025 → 19.2% Q2 2026 → 18.3% Q3 2026) on higher lot/construction costs and pricing pressure, with no floor stated by management -- the single most-watched line in the thesis. Lots controlled holding up while margin falls shows NVR is choosing to keep optioning land rather than pulling back, i.e. it still expects to build that supply eventually.

What to watch:

  • Whether margin compression stabilises or keeps falling quarter over quarter
  • Lots controlled per active community (land bank depth) trending down, which would signal a deliberate pullback

mortgage.title: Mortgage banking volume and capture rate
mortgage.content:
Mortgage loan volume is dollars originated by NVR Mortgage Finance; capture rate is the share of NVR's own homebuyers who finance through it rather than an outside lender.

For NVR: NVRM only ever serves NVR's own buyers, so loan volume is capped by (and tracks) homebuilding closings -- it is not an independent growth driver. The segment's profit lever is capture rate and gain-on-sale margin, not loan growth; Q3 2026 segment profit improved even as volume fell, on better margins and a mix shift toward ARM products.

What to watch:

  • Capture rate drifting down (buyers using outside lenders, a sign of less-competitive rates or terms)
  • Loan volume falling faster than homebuilding closings (a timing or mix issue, not demand)

segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue: geography and mortgage banking
segmentRevenue.content:
Homebuilding revenue split across NVR's four reporting regions -- Mid Atlantic (MD/VA/DC/DE/WV), South East (NC/SC/GA/FL/TN/KY), Mid East (NY/OH/western PA/IN/IL) and North East (NJ/eastern PA) -- plus mortgage banking fee/gain-on-sale revenue.

For NVR: Mid Atlantic is the largest region at roughly 43% of FY2025 homebuilding revenue, South East about 26%, Mid East about 19% and North East about 12% -- there is no West Coast or Mountain West exposure, so this chart is the whole of NVR's geographic diversification (or lack of it).

What to watch:

  • Any region declining faster than the group average (a local demand or affordability problem, not a national one)
  • Mortgage banking revenue tracking homebuilding revenue, since it is structurally dependent on it

segmentProfit.title: Segment profit: geography and mortgage banking
segmentProfit.content:
Segment-level profit (before corporate overhead and tax) for the same four homebuilding regions plus mortgage banking's own operating income.

For NVR: read this beside the segment revenue chart -- a region whose profit falls faster than its revenue is losing margin, not just volume, which is the more important signal in a downturn. Mortgage banking's operating income is a useful cross-check: when it holds up or improves while homebuilding segment profit falls (as in Q3 2026), the weakness is on the house-building side, not financing.

What to watch:

  • Any region's profit margin (profit / revenue from the two charts together) falling furthest
  • Mortgage banking profit diverging from homebuilding profit, which points to where the pressure actually sits

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For NVR, Inc.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For NVR, Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
